exposure_definition: Household location inside an irrigation-district (ID) jurisdiction boundary within a Disadvantaged Community census place (ID-DAC), vs. outside irrigation-district jurisdiction (General DAC, GDC) -- i.e. legal/institutional membership in an irrigation district under California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) framework and >150 years of California water-rights law.
comparator_definition: DAC census places located outside irrigation-district jurisdiction (GDC, n=56).
effect_measure: percentage_comparison_with_p_value (unadjusted group comparison)
effect_estimate: Poor drinking-water exposure (CalEnviroScreen 4.0 indicator): 83% (ID-DAC, n=97) vs 79% (GDC, n=56), p=0.1363; overall DAC vulnerability 83% vs 81%, p=0.3147; median household income $34,276 vs $36,450, p=0.7893.
direction: null (no statistically significant difference at conventional thresholds)
adjusted: unadjusted
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S037; source Espinoza & Viers 2024, PLOS Water, Table 1. Null result recorded faithfully -- the paper's own quantitative test does not show a statistically significant effect of irrigation-district legal membership on household drinking-water outcomes, despite its qualitative/policy narrative emphasizing inequity.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 decision tree -- single study defining this exact exposure-comparator (irrigation-district legal membership); no other Family A study yet shares this operationalization of legal recognition, so pooling is not yet possible or meaningful (too few independent studies in this family, per PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 Family A guidance).

exposure_definition: Random offer of a targeted sanitation subsidy to households determined eligible via the Poverty Probability Index for Cambodia and a climate-vulnerability threshold (service/subsidy eligibility mechanism).
comparator_definition: Eligible households not offered the subsidy / ineligible households in treatment areas (sales closing rate 6%).
effect_measure: percentage_point_difference (randomized controlled trial, intent-to-treat)
effect_estimate: Subsidy offer increased likelihood of climate-resilient latrine purchase by 32 percentage points; sales closing rate 38% (eligible/treatment) vs 6% (ineligible/treatment).
sample_size: clustered RCT; 30 villages in Kampong Chhnang province, Cambodia (23 climate-vulnerable; treatment and control halves), 2,821 sales presentations (full text read 2026-10-04)
direction: positive (subsidy eligibility increases sanitation-product purchase)
adjusted: unadjusted (intent-to-treat comparison as reported in study highlights)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S057; source Kozole et al. 2023, J. Water Sanitation & Hygiene for Development. Strongest causal design in the eligible corpus (clustered RCT) for a Family A eligibility mechanism. Full text read 2026-10-04: the abstract gives the effect as 32 percentage points and the highlights as 31%; both are reported here as in the text (process_drive_inbox_2026-10-04b.py).
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single RCT; no other Family A study shares this subsidy-eligibility operationalization or a convertible common estimand (percentage-point difference here vs. OR/RR elsewhere); too few independent, comparably-operationalized studies to pool.

exposure_definition: Household's slum-settlement legal notification status under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act 1971 (notified vs. non-notified), following the 2014 Bombay High Court order in Pani Haq Samiti v. Brihan Mumbai Municipal Corporation.
comparator_definition: Notified households (legally recognized settlements).
effect_measure: % difference in log-transformed water quantity (LPCD), adjusted multivariate linear regression
effect_estimate: Non-notified households used 37.3% fewer litres per capita per day than notified households (adjusted); 38.2% fewer unadjusted; 38.7% of the association mediated by infrastructure/accessibility/cost/reliability factors (GSEM path analysis).
direction: negative (non-notified/unrecognized status associated with lower water access)
adjusted: adjusted (household size, income per capita, religion)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S084; source Lubeck-Schricker et al. 2023, Environment & Urbanization. Authors note cross-sectional design cannot establish causality (mechanism_certainty=1); notification status not randomly/quasi-experimentally assigned.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single study for this legal-notification-status exposure-comparator; S085 shares the same Mumbai/Bombay High Court legal backdrop but tests a different exposure (bureaucratic assistance x political coordination, not notification status itself) and a different outcome (formalization, not LPCD), so the two are not poolable together without manufacturing comparability; too few independent studies sharing this exact operationalization to pool.

exposure_definition: Random assignment to bureaucratic-assistance treatment (T1: help completing formalization application/paperwork) crossed with political-coordination treatment (T2), in a 2x2 factorial cluster-randomized field experiment on informal-settlement land formalization in Mumbai.
comparator_definition: Control households receiving neither T1 nor T2 (usual/unassisted formalization procedure).
effect_measure: marginal effect (percentage points), weighted least squares regression with T1xT2 interaction, block fixed effects, cluster-robust SE
effect_estimate: In the eligible-lands sample, T1 (bureaucratic assistance) increased full formalization by 19 percentage points (~45% of control mean) when combined with T2 (political coordination); T1xT2 interaction coefficient .22 (eligible-lands sample); full-sample interaction .11 (not significant). T1 alone raised application submission/inspection-visit likelihood but not full formalization; T2 alone had no significant average effect.
direction: positive (bureaucratic assistance increases formalization, conditional on political coordination)
adjusted: unadjusted (main specification; no covariates beyond block fixed effects)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S085; source Gaikwad & Thomas 2026, AJPS. Extraction note explicitly identifies this as "a clean empirical match to PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 candidate meta-analytic Family B," but flags that the bureaucratic-assistance effect operates only jointly with political coordination -- a genuine complication for treating Family B as a simple main effect. Strongest-design study in the extraction set (cluster-randomized field experiment).
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single study for Family B; PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 itself flags Family B's study count may be too small to pool ("use structured quantitative synthesis if so"); no second study with a comparable bureaucratic-assistance-vs-usual-procedure contrast yet in the corpus.

exposure_definition: Household home-ownership / tenure status (owner vs. non-owner) in a multilevel household-neighbourhood-provider model of piped-water intermittency, alongside provider-level institutional capacity (utility GDP per capita) as a covariate.
comparator_definition: Non-owner households (renters/other tenure).
effect_measure: multilevel logistic regression, adjusted odds ratio (OR)
effect_estimate: Home ownership associated with higher odds of reporting water-supply interruption (OR=1.31, p<0.01), controlling for provider and other household/neighbourhood covariates; overall 47% (95% CI 45-49%) of piped households reported >=1 full day of unavailability in the prior fortnight, ranging 18-76% across providers.
direction: positive (home ownership associated with higher odds of interruption -- direction counter to a simple "tenure security improves access" hypothesis)
adjusted: adjusted (multilevel model controlling for provider, ethnicity proxy, season, neighbourhood wealth, neighbour-tap use, utility GDP per capita)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S104; source Thomas-Possee et al. 2024, PLOS Water. Flagged with caution: this is a multivariable risk-factor study without one single hypothesis-driven exposure -- home ownership is extracted here as the closest tenure/property-status exposure to Family A's "formal vs. informal tenure" definition, but the study's own framing treats it as one covariate among several, not a dedicated legal-recognition test. Do not treat as a like-for-like replication of S084/S085's notification-status exposure.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- exposure only loosely comparable to other Family A studies' tenure/recognition definitions (see provenance_note caveat); direction of effect also runs counter to S084's notified-status finding, so pooling would risk manufacturing comparability across non-equivalent exposures per PROJECT_SPEC.md S8's core rule.

exposure_definition: Municipal incorporation status (incorporated vs. unincorporated), which functions as the legal/jurisdictional eligibility gateway to centralized municipal water/wastewater service extension in the U.S.
comparator_definition: Incorporated census block groups.
effect_measure: negative binomial regression, incidence rate ratio
effect_estimate: Unincorporated status and poverty rate are significantly associated with reduced centralized water/wastewater infrastructure access; sewer coverage rates significantly lower for unincorporated communities near municipal boundaries, consistent with municipal underbounding excluding these areas from service-area expansion. Full-text check 2026-10-04 (main text; the confidence intervals are in Supplementary Tables 5-6, which are not in the PDF): among high-poverty block groups, unincorporated status is associated with 3.54 times the unsewered land area and 17.8 times the area unserved by centralized water (incidence rate ratios); among block groups without high poverty, 1.48 times the unsewered area; for high-poverty Outlying and Island communities the IRR for unsewered area exceeds 4.0, while Outlying communities without high poverty have IRR 0.91.
direction: negative (unincorporated/unrecognized jurisdictional status associated with reduced service access)
adjusted: adjusted (multivariate negative binomial regression controlling for poverty rate, proximity to municipal boundary, regional/state indicators)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S142; source Allaire et al. 2024, npj Clean Water. Large-N administrative dataset; observational/cross-sectional, not quasi-experimental (mechanism_certainty=2). Full text read 2026-10-04 (npj Clean Water 7:125): sample 31,383 block groups in nine states confirmed; narrative direction confirmed; IRRs added from the main text (process_drive_inbox_2026-10-04.py).
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single study; the incidence rate ratios printed in the main text (3.54, 17.8, 1.48) were recorded on 2026-10-04 from the full text, but their confidence intervals are in supplementary tables that were not available, the outcomes are land-area ratios (not odds ratios or percentage differences), and S037/S084/S057 measure different estimands, so no common metric exists -- left unpooled rather than approximated, per PROJECT_SPEC.md S14.

exposure_definition: Women's meaningful participation in Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSC) governance (participation vs. non-participation), propensity-score-matched.
comparator_definition: Non-participating households/women (PSM-matched comparison group).
effect_measure: propensity score matching (PSM)-estimated average treatment effect
effect_estimate: VWSC participation improved toilet functionality by 24.8%, reduced water-collection time by 31.4 minutes, and lowered illness incidence by 12.7% (PSM-estimated); distance to water source was the strongest predictor of time burden (beta=0.62, p<0.001).
direction: positive (participation improves access-related outcomes)
adjusted: adjusted (PSM-estimated causal effects)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S149; source Sethy & Sahoo 2026, Discover Public Health. Participation in local water-governance committees is a citizen-side accommodation/participation mechanism, distinct from Family B's provider-side "bureaucratic assistance" (which describes officials helping applicants navigate procedure, not citizens participating in local governance bodies) -- does not cleanly match Family A, B, or C's exposure definitions as written in PROJECT_SPEC.md S8.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- exposure (community-governance participation) does not match any of the three existing synthesis families' definitions; recorded here as a pooling-candidate flag rather than assigned a family, per DATA_DICTIONARY.md's allowance for "a newly identified family" -- no new family has been formally defined in 05_analysis/meta_analysis/ yet, so this single study does not justify creating one.

exposure_definition: Municipal institutional capacity (financial, technical, political, and operational capacity, derived via exploratory factor analysis) -- weaker capacity treated as a proxy for administrative/implementation barriers to sanitation universalization.
comparator_definition: Municipalities with higher institutional-capacity factor scores.
effect_measure: multiple linear regression with robust correction (following exploratory factor analysis)
effect_estimate: Full-text coefficients per capacity factor-score unit (robust SE; p), N = 391: water coverage -- financial 6.02 (1.02), technical 2.67 (0.99), operational 2.41 (0.92), political (plan/policy under Law 11,445/2007) -1.89 (0.88; p = 0.033); sewerage -- financial 7.36, technical 3.94, operational 13.07, political -0.66 (p = 0.687); solid-waste collection -- financial 10.06, technical 2.25 (p = 0.078), operational 28.26, political +2.56 (p = 0.055). Financial, technical and operational capacity are positively associated with coverage; the legal-compliance (plan/policy) component is not.
sample_size: 574 Minas Gerais municipalities (outliers removed); 391 in the final models; 2018 cross-section
direction: positive (higher institutional capacity associated with better sanitation-access indicators)
adjusted: adjusted (multiple linear regression with robust correction)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S174; source de Araujo, Ferreira & da Rocha, "Capacidades institucionais para a universalizacao do acesso ao saneamento basico." Ecological/municipality-level analysis; institutional-capacity-as-barrier-proxy is a looser reading of Family C's "administrative barriers" exposure than a directly measured barrier (e.g. a documentation requirement or eligibility restriction) -- flagged as an approximate rather than exact fit. UPDATED 2026-10-04 from the full text: Minas Gerais only (not national), n = 391, coefficients above; the direction column is the composite reading (3 of 4 capacity dimensions positive for every outcome) -- the political/legal-plan dimension is negative for water, null for sewerage, marginally positive for waste.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single study; coefficients are per standardised factor-score unit with outcomes in percentage points of coverage and are not comparable with other Family C measures, so they cannot be pooled; PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 flags Family C as conceptually attractive but potentially too heterogeneous (secondary synthesis), and a single ecological study does not meet that bar.

exposure_definition: Presence/intensity of Water Safety Plan (WSP) water-quality regulatory programming (an enforcement/regulatory mechanism), compared across repeated cross-sectional survey waves (2016 vs. 2017) in southern Syria.
comparator_definition: Survey wave/area without WSP programming in place (pre-WSP baseline, 2016).
effect_measure: mixed-effect logistic regression, adjusted odds ratio (mOR)
effect_estimate: Free chlorine residual (FCR) >0.1 mg/L increased from 4.1% to 27.9% (2016-2017), strongly associated with WSP programming (mOR 24.16, 95% CI 5.93-98.5); piped water as main source declined 22.0% to 15.3%; childhood diarrhea prevalence declined 32.8% to 20.4%.
direction: positive (WSP regulatory programming associated with improved water-quality outcome)
adjusted: adjusted (mixed-effect logistic regression)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S178; source Sikder et al. 2018, Conflict and Health. Outcome measured is water quality (chlorine residual) and diarrhea prevalence, not a formal-connection/access-quantity outcome as defined for Families A-C in PROJECT_SPEC.md S8; recorded as a pooling-candidate flag rather than forced into an existing family.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- outcome (water-quality regulatory compliance in a humanitarian/conflict setting) is not comparable to the formal-connection/access outcomes used elsewhere in Families A-C; population/context (protracted-conflict Syria) also not comparable to the largely non-conflict settings of the other candidate studies -- pooling would manufacture comparability that does not exist.

exposure_definition: Random assignment to a community-driven WASH intervention with an institutional-strengthening component (formation/training of community WASH committees), cluster-randomized at the village level in rural DRC.
comparator_definition: Control villages (no intervention).
effect_measure: intention-to-treat analysis, cluster-randomized controlled trial, adjusted mean differences
effect_estimate: No effect on diarrhea (adjusted mean difference -0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.03) or length-for-age Z-score (adjusted mean difference -0.01, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.12); intervention villages scored 0.40 points higher (95% CI 0.16-0.65) on an index of community WASH institutions.
direction: null (health outcomes); positive (institutional-strengthening outcome)
adjusted: adjusted (intention-to-treat, cluster-randomized)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S294; source Quattrochi et al. 2025, PLOS Medicine. Institutional-strengthening component (WASH-institutions index result) is the Family-B-relevant finding; health outcomes (diarrhea, LAZ) are null and belong to a different estimand (health, not access/formalization) -- recorded together here for completeness but should not be pooled together even within this single study's own results, per PROJECT_SPEC.md S8's caution against mixing estimands.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single cluster-RCT; no other Family B study yet measures a comparable "community WASH institutions index" outcome (S085 measures individual land-formalization instead), so the two are not poolable together without manufacturing comparability across different outcome constructs.

exposure_definition: Community water system (CWS) ownership type: privately owned vs. publicly owned, in Virginia's Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) regulatory-compliance regime (2006-2016).
comparator_definition: Publicly owned CWSs.
effect_measure: negative binomial regression, adjusted odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval
effect_estimate: Privately owned CWSs had 90% higher odds of a Monitoring & Reporting (MR) violation than publicly owned CWSs (OR=1.899, 95% CI 1.455-2.478). (The study also reports a separate, real effect for %Black population on Health-Based violations, OR=1.031 [1.018-1.045] per 1-percentage-point increase, and for system size on MR violations -- ownership type is recorded here as the clearest single legal/institutional exposure-comparator per CODEBOOK.md S12's one-prespecified-effect-per-study default; the race-based finding was not used as the primary effect for the same reason S135 was excluded from this file entirely -- population demographic composition is not itself a legal/institutional exposure.)
direction: positive (private ownership associated with higher odds of a monitoring/reporting violation)
adjusted: adjusted (negative binomial regression, LASSO-selected covariates: race/ethnicity, %homeownership, %65+, rurality, system size, source, year)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S353; source Marcillo, Krometis & Krometis 2021, IJERPH 18(24):13254, Table 1. Ownership type (private/public) is a real institutional/regulatory-model variable, but does not cleanly match Family A (household-level legal recognition/tenure), Family B (bureaucratic assistance to applicants), or Family C (a specific documented administrative barrier such as a fee or eligibility rule) as defined in PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 -- it is a provider-level ownership-structure characteristic predicting regulatory-compliance outcomes, not a household-facing legal/administrative barrier. Recorded without a family assignment rather than forced into one.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- exposure (utility ownership type) does not match any existing synthesis family's definition; no other study in the corpus tests the same private-vs-public-ownership contrast on a comparable regulatory-violation outcome, so pooling is not possible even in principle yet.

exposure_definition: Tribal oversight/primacy regulatory jurisdiction over groundwater management, vs. state-primacy regulatory jurisdiction, across 1,881 groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas in Arizona.
comparator_definition: State-primacy regulatory jurisdiction areas.
effect_measure: multivariate regression, adjusted odds ratio (OR)
effect_estimate: Tribal oversight significantly reduced groundwater decline risk (OR=0.62, p<0.001), while state-primacy areas showed mixed effects on the same outcome. (The study also reports real ORs for racial/ethnic population composition -- OR=2.01 for higher-Black-population communities, OR=0.92 for Hispanic/Latino communities, both p<0.001 -- but per the same reasoning that excluded S135 from this file, population demographic composition is not itself a legal/institutional exposure, so Tribal-oversight jurisdiction is recorded here as the primary effect instead.)
direction: negative/protective (Tribal oversight jurisdiction associated with lower odds of groundwater decline)
adjusted: adjusted (multivariate regression controlling for race/ethnicity, gender composition, age 65+, household/family structure, institutional/migrant-worker housing, designated-management-area status)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S358; source Williams et al. 2025, Water 17(7):1097. Tribal oversight/primacy is a genuine jurisdictional legal-recognition variable (which government has regulatory authority) directly analogous to PROJECT_SPEC.md S8 Family A's 'legal recognition and access' framing, though it operates at the level of environmental/water-resource regulatory authority rather than household tenure or service-eligibility status as in S084/S085/S142 -- flagged as a looser fit than those three, not a like-for-like replication. A26 ruling 2026-10-14 by CK: moved from Family A to the reasoned non-fits; the outcome is groundwater decline and contamination risk at the level of 1,881 groundwater-supplied service areas (aquifer availability), not household connection, access or service quality.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md section 2 decision tree and PROJECT_SPEC.md section 8: reasoned non-fit, no family assigned (A26 ruling 2026-10-14 by CK, formerly Family A): the outcome is groundwater decline and contamination risk at the level of 1,881 groundwater-supplied service areas (aquifer availability), not household connection, access or service quality, so it does not match Family A, B or C. It is a single study with this exposure (Tribal oversight against state primacy) and this outcome, so pooling is not possible.

exposure_definition: Water point maintained by a local authority (institutional/governance management arrangement), vs. water point with no management arrangement at all.
comparator_definition: Water points with No Management (no institutional/governance body responsible for maintenance).
effect_measure: adjusted odds ratio (multivariable logistic regression)
effect_estimate: Local management vs No Management: adjusted OR = 3.733 for water-point functionality.
direction: positive (institutional/local management associated with higher odds of functionality)
adjusted: adjusted (multivariable logistic regression controlling for repair time, mechanic/toolkit availability, payment status, water availability, spare-parts-supplier distance, damage status, county)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S388; source Li, McManus & Cronk 2025, Sustainability 17(19):8928, Table 5. Genuine institutional/governance-management exposure (who is responsible for a water point's maintenance) vs. a real comparator (no management), with a locatable adjusted OR and 95% CI from a large administrative census (n=11,065). synthesis_family left blank rather than forced into Family A/B/C: the exposure is institutional management CAPACITY/responsibility-assignment, not quite legal recognition/tenure (Family A), application-process bureaucratic assistance (Family B), or a barrier restricting access (Family C) -- a real judgment call, not a mechanical fit, so left for a human/manuscript-stage decision rather than guessed. Two further comparator categories (Institutional vs No Management, adjusted OR=2.893, 95% CI 2.349-3.562; WASH Committee vs No Management, adjusted OR=2.426, 95% CI 1.946-3.026) are available in the source but not used as the primary effect here, per CODEBOOK.md S12's one-prespecified-effect-per-study default -- Local vs No Management was selected as the strongest and most policy-emphasized of the three (highlighted first in the paper's own abstract).
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 decision tree -- single study defining this exact exposure-comparator (local-authority management vs no management for Liberian hand pumps); no other included study yet shares this operationalization, so pooling is not yet possible or meaningful.

exposure_definition: Household census-tract location within an area designated ZEIS (Zona Especial de Interesse Social / Social Interest Special Zone) in Recife, Brazil -- a legal/institutional zoning-eligibility status conferred under municipal ZEIS legislation (Municipal Land Use Law 14,511/83, PREZEIS Municipal Law 14,947/87, as amended) to areas meeting statutory low-income/informality criteria.
comparator_definition: Matched census tracts not subject to ZEIS designation, before/after the intervention (difference-in-differences).
effect_measure: difference-in-differences (DiD) percentage-point estimate
effect_estimate: ZEIS designation associated with an approximately 23 percentage-point increase in the share of households with sewage-network access, 14-17 years after implementation (~150% increase over the 1991 baseline level); also significant positive effects on water-network access and homeownership rate; no significant effect on bathrooms per household or garbage-collection access.
sample_size: census-tract panel, Recife, 1991/2000/2010 (962 census tracts in 1991)
direction: positive (ZEIS designation associated with increased water/sewage-network access and homeownership)
adjusted: adjusted (difference-in-differences with census-tract fixed effects; robust across multiple control-group definitions and econometric specifications)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S398; source dos Santos Nascimento Sobrinho & da Mota Silveira Neto 2025, Nova Economia 35(3):e8355. A genuine Family A (legal recognition/eligibility) exposure -- ZEIS zoning-law designation, a real legal/institutional eligibility status defined by statute -- with a real quasi-experimental (DiD) comparator and a locatable, non-fabricated percentage-point effect estimate from official IBGE census panel data. Exact numeric coefficients/standard errors for the water/sewage-access DiD estimates were not located in the extracted abstract/results-narrative text (only the ~23-percentage-point sewage figure and directional/significance findings were reported in the pages read); the full regression-output table was not retrieved in this pass.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 decision tree -- single study defining this exact exposure-comparator (ZEIS zoning-law designation vs non-ZEIS census tracts, Recife); no other included Family A study shares this operationalization, so pooling is not yet possible or meaningful.

exposure_definition: Household membership in a Water Resource Users' Association (WRUA), a legal collective-action institution established under Kenya's Water Act 2002/2016
comparator_definition: Household non-membership in a WRUA (no formal legal water-governance institutional status)
effect_measure: Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT), water poverty index
effect_estimate: -0.14 to -0.32 (14% to 32% reduction in water poverty), depending on estimator (endogenous switching probit: -14%; inverse probability weighting: -30%; propensity score matching: -32%)
direction: WRUA membership reduces water poverty
adjusted: TRUE (endogenous switching regression and matching methods correcting for non-random selection into WRUA membership)
provenance_note: Mwaura et al. 2021, Ewaso Ng'iro North Catchment Area, Kenya; effect consistent in direction and approximate magnitude across three independent quasi-experimental estimators (ESP, PSM, IPW); p<0.05 across all three per the study.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: Single study for this specific exposure-comparator definition (WRUA legal membership vs. non-membership); no other study in the corpus shares a comparable estimand -- ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 decision tree not yet cleared for any family.

exposure_definition: Household located within a 50 km radius of an active mining site, Africa (proximity-based exposure to local economic/institutional activity associated with mining).
comparator_definition: Households outside the 50 km active-mine radius (including households near inactive/closed mines).
effect_measure: instrumental-variable regression, percentage-point difference in self-reported probability
effect_estimate: Households within 50 km of an active mine reported a 4 percentage-point lower probability of lacking clean water, supported by IV estimates as a causal effect; robust local institutions were found to further moderate (strengthen) this water-security benefit.
direction: positive (active-mine proximity associated with reduced probability of lacking clean water)
adjusted: TRUE (instrumental-variable regression with household/regional covariates)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S434; source Frempong, Stadelmann & Thiam 2025, Applied Economic Perspectives and Policy. Institutional-strength (local governance) moderation of this effect is reported narratively in the source but not as a separate numeric interaction coefficient in the retrieved text, so only the primary 4-percentage-point IV estimate is recorded here.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md §2 decision tree -- re-examined 2026-09-28 against PROJECT_SPEC.md §8's Family A/B/C definitions (the same pass that resolved this row's 8 siblings, S435/S445/S448/S470/S471/S483/S489/S491, left blank without a documented family-fit judgment in the batches that added them). This study's exposure is proximity to an active mining site -- an economic/geographic exposure, not a legal or administrative mechanism at all. It does not match Family A (legal recognition/tenure/eligibility), Family B (bureaucratic assistance/procedural simplification), or Family C (legal or administrative barriers, documentation, eligibility restrictions, formalization barriers). The source discusses local institutional strength as a moderator of this effect, but only narratively -- no separate numeric interaction coefficient was retrievable (see provenance_note), so there is no institutional/legal estimate here to classify in the first place. synthesis_family is left blank as a reasoned non-fit, not an omission -- single study for this exposure-comparator in any case, so pooling would not yet be possible even if a family did apply.

exposure_definition: Brazilian rural public elementary school located in the North region (a region with a substantially lower Municipal Human Development Index-Income and higher rural-population share) -- a proxy for weaker municipal fiscal/institutional capacity to invest in school WASH infrastructure under the PDDE's enrolment-based, not needs-based, funding formula.
comparator_definition: Schools located in the Center-West region (reference category).
effect_measure: binomial logistic regression, adjusted odds ratio (OR)
effect_estimate: Odds of a school lacking water supply were OR=2.58 (p<0.001) in 2011, rising to OR=6.40 (p<0.001) in 2023, for North-region schools vs. Center-West reference; odds of lacking sanitation were OR=3.32 (p<0.001) in 2011 and OR=5.48 (p<0.001) in 2023.
sample_size: 56,544 rural public elementary schools (2011); 34,406 rural public elementary schools (2023); national School Census microdata
direction: positive (North-region location associated with higher odds of lacking water/sanitation services, i.e. worse access)
adjusted: TRUE (binomial logistic regression controlling for indigenous-land location, school size, dropout/pass rates, municipal rural-population share and municipal HDI-income)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S445; source Medeiros et al., Cadernos de Saude Publica (Portuguese full-text web-snapshot located among the 15 ambiguous-filename Google Docs; DOI 10.1590/0102-311XPT128025). Several further region/indigenous-land/school-size odds ratios are reported in the same source (see extraction_database.csv effect_estimate) but per CODEBOOK.md S12's one-prespecified-effect-per-study default, the North-vs-Center-West water-absence odds ratio is recorded here as the primary effect, being both the largest-magnitude and most consistently significant across both study years.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md §2 -- re-examined 2026-09-28 (see S434's note for the batch context). effect_estimate: OR=2.125 (95% CI 1.581-2.857, p<0.001) -- households that do not normally buy/pay for water have roughly double the odds of being unwilling to pay for water during the lockdown-era disconnection moratorium, relative to households with an existing formal payment relationship.
sample_size: 1,639 households (40 small towns, 4 regions of Uganda)
direction: positive (lack of an existing formal payment relationship with the water utility is associated with higher odds of unwillingness to pay during the disconnection-moratorium period)

exposure_definition: Degree to which a Prussian city's local franchise/voting-rights system concentrated political power among the wealthiest taxpayers (the tax-weighted 'Three Class System', in force in the Rhineland and Westphalia) versus a more equal, tax-based franchise (Hannover and Holstein), 1880-1887.
comparator_definition: Cities under the more equal-franchise systems of Hannover and Holstein, and within-province variation in the skewness of the local income/tax distribution (SKEW variable).
effect_measure: Logit regression coefficient and predicted-probability responsiveness, with counterfactual provincial coefficient-swap simulations
effect_estimate: SKEW (income/tax-payment skew) coefficient 0.457 in the Three-Class-System provinces (responsiveness 0.175); likelihood-ratio test rejects the null that franchise structure did not matter (test statistic -30.0, 3 df, significant at all conventional levels). Counterfactual: imposing Hannover's (equal-franchise) coefficients on Westphalian towns lowers their average predicted probability of building a waterworks by about one-third; imposing Holstein's coefficients reduces it to zero; conversely, imposing Rhineland's (Three-Class-System) coefficients on non-building towns in Hannover/Holstein substantially raises predicted probability.
sample_size: 244 cities (50 building, 194 not building waterworks during 1880-1887)
direction: positive (greater concentration of local political power among wealthy taxpayers/property owners associated with a higher probability of a city investing in waterworks infrastructure)
adjusted: adjusted (instrumented cost per capita; controls for community ability to pay, cholera mortality, population density, and industrial/steel employment)

exposure_definition: Administrative district legal/institutional classification (si, urban-type, coded 1) versus gun (rural-type, coded 0) among South Korean local governments, 2010/2016/2021, alongside municipal fiscal autonomy (degree of financial independence, i.e. own-source revenue share of general accounting revenue) and local tax burden per person (log).

effect_estimate: Administrative district unit (si=1): significant NEGATIVE coefficient (improves equity) in 2021 on average unit price (-0.9174, p<0.01), cost-recovery rate (-0.9064, p<0.05), revenue-water ratio (-0.8489, p<0.05), water-supply rate (-0.8566, p<0.01), and number of employees (-1.1569, p<0.01); not significant for customer satisfaction. Local tax burden per person (log): significant NEGATIVE coefficient (improves equity) on all 6 variables at p<0.01 in all 3 years (e.g. average unit price 2021: -1.9115). exposure_definition: Share of a Chinese prefectural city's population who are temporary residents without official permanent household registration (hukou) -- a legal/administrative status ascribed at birth that determines eligibility for place-specific public services -- measured across 290 cities, 2008-2014.

sample_size: 290 cities; 1,577-1,769 city-year observations across 5 outcome models (2008-2014)
direction: negative (higher hukou-unregistered temporary-resident share associated with lower per-capita pollution-treatment infrastructure provision)
adjusted: adjusted (population density, GRP per capita, education enrollment, unemployment rate, government spending per capita; city and year fixed effects)

It is a single study with this exposure (the share of hukou-unregistered residents) and this outcome, so pooling is not possible.

exposure_definition: Creation of a new local government (kabupaten/kota) via pemekaran -- the legal/administrative splitting of an existing district jurisdiction into smaller administrative units -- in Indonesia's post-2001 decentralization era, exploiting the plausibly exogenous timing of district-splitting decisions as the identifying exposure.
comparator_definition: Original (non-split) parent districts, and separately, sibling split-off districts, all within the same national panel of 336 kabupaten/kota, 2001-2014.
effect_measure: Generalized difference-in-differences regression coefficient (static model) and two-step dynamic panel GMM regression coefficient with district-clustered standard errors
effect_estimate: New-district creation reduces household access to protected water and sanitation by approximately 1% in year 2 relative to original districts (static DiD model) and by approximately 1.35 percentage points in the second year of operation (dynamic GMM model), implying a long-run reduction of approximately 1.75% (beta/(1-gamma) = -1.35/(1-0.23)), p=.023. No significant contemporaneous or lagged effect relative to split-off (sibling) districts, and no significant effect on school enrollment in either comparison. Falsification tests using first and second leads of the new-district dummy show no significant pre-trend, supporting the parallel-trends assumption.
sample_size: 336 districts (98 groups for split-vs-new comparison); 2,714 district-year observations (infrastructure equation, original-vs-new comparison)
direction: negative (local government proliferation associated with LOWER household water/sanitation access, relative to original non-split districts)
adjusted: adjusted (total local government spending per capita, population size, percentage of households with electricity access, percentage of population in poverty, Gini coefficient of personal consumption, personal consumption per capita; district and year fixed effects, district-specific time trends; dynamic model additionally instruments the lagged dependent variable via two-step difference-GMM)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S631; source Lewis 2017, Journal of Urban Affairs 39(8):1047-1065, Tables 4-5. A clean legal/administrative-jurisdictional-restructuring exposure (local government proliferation via pemekaran) tested by a well-identified quasi-experimental panel design (generalized DiD plus dynamic GMM, parallel-trends falsification test) against a directly measured, nationally-representative household water/sanitation access-percentage outcome (BPS/SUSENAS), with a statistically significant long-run point estimate.
exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single quantitative study using an Indonesia-specific administrative-jurisdiction-splitting exposure and a household water/sanitation access-percentage outcome; no other Family C study in the corpus shares this specific institutional/legal operationalization (local government proliferation/pemekaran), so pooling is not yet possible or meaningful.

exposure_definition: Participation in Indonesia's Water Hibah (WH) intergovernmental performance-grant program -- a fiscal/administrative mechanism under which a kabupaten/kota (local government) makes an equity investment in its PDAM (local water enterprise), which the PDAM uses to establish household water connections for the poor, triggering a Ministry of Finance transfer (Rp 2 million per connection for the first 1,000, Rp 3 million thereafter) once connections are verified operational.
comparator_definition: Matched control kabupaten/kota not participating in the Water Hibah program in 2010-2011, drawn via one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching from a pool of 65 local governments subsequently added to the program in 2013.
effect_measure: Propensity-score-matched treatment/control OLS regression and hurdle-model regression (probit selection equation plus conditional linear regression, bootstrapped standard errors, endogenous-transfer instrumentation)
effect_estimate: WH program participation increases per capita PDAM equity investment by Rp 739 in constant 2000 terms (Rp 2,141 in 2010-11 terms), coefficient 739.1, z=3.20, p<0.05. WH-financed investment per capita is a significant positive determinant of new household water connections per 1,000 persons: coefficient 0.0003 (t=6.16, investment treated as exogenous) / 0.0004 (t=1.71, investment treated as endogenous), both significant at conventional levels. Estimated marginal cost of a WH-financed connection is Rp 2.5-2.9 million versus Rp 6.9-8.2 million for a connection financed from other local-government revenue sources -- a statistically significant difference in cost-efficiency. The WH program-participation dummy itself is not significant once WH-financed investment is separately specified, indicating the grant's effect on connections operates through the financed-investment channel rather than participation per se.
sample_size: 35 treatment + 35 control kabupaten/kota (34 after common-support trimming); 105 pooled local-government-year observations, 2010-2011
direction: positive (Water Hibah program participation and grant-financed investment associated with HIGHER household water connections, relative to non-participating matched local governments)
adjusted: adjusted (log of other revenues per capita, log population, percentage of population urban, percentage of population poor, lagged percentage of population with access to water, log gross regional domestic product per capita; propensity-score-matched treatment/control sample; on/off-Java and year instruments for the endogenous WH-transfer specification)
provenance_note: extraction_database.csv S636; source Lewis 2014, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies 50(3):415-433, Tables 5-10. exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 -- single quantitative study using an Indonesia-specific intergovernmental fiscal-transfer/performance-grant exposure and a household water-connection outcome; the exposure (a fiscal grant conditioning PDAM equity investment) does not cleanly match PROJECT_SPEC.md S8's Family A (legal recognition/tenure/eligibility), Family B (bureaucratic assistance/procedural simplification), or Family C (legal/administrative barriers) definitions, and no other quantitative study in the corpus shares this specific fiscal-grant operationalization, so pooling is not yet possible or meaningful.

standard_error: 0.0126 (indigenous coefficient, coverage model); 0.001 (indigenous coefficient, transfers model); 0.2437 (transfers coefficient, coverage model)

exposure_definition: Private (vs. public) ownership of a Brazilian water and sanitation business corporation -- a governance-structure/institutional variable -- tested alongside presence/type of economic regulatory agency (local vs. regional vs. unregulated) and regulatory regime (rate-of-return, price-cap/revenue-cap, vs. municipally-negotiated tariff).

Local/regional regulatory-agency coefficients negative but not significant (H2 rejected). Rate-of-return and price-cap/revenue-cap regulatory-regime coefficients not significant relative to municipally-negotiated tariffs (H3 rejected).

adjusted: adjusted (OPEX, capital expenditure (depreciation and return components), government investment subsidies, tariff-block structure, water-quality/service-quality indicators, sewage treatment, average water consumption, GDP per capita, regional fixed effects)

exclusion_from_pooling_reason: ANALYSIS_PLAN.md S2 decision tree -- re-examined 2026-09-28 as part of the Phase 11 corpus-level family judgment: this study's exposure (private vs. public/mixed-capital utility ownership) and outcome (a tariff/price-level measure) are the same KIND of comparison already recorded under Family C for S526 (private ownership vs. unit-price-ratio progressivity, US) and S539 (private ownership vs. annual household bill/income-share, US) -- leaving this row's synthesis_family blank while S526/S539 carry 'C' for the same ownership-vs-price pairing was an inconsistency, not a principled distinction, so it is corrected to Family C here. exposure_definition: Randomized assignment to systematic contract enforcement (transparent, credible service-disconnection notices for nonpayment, per the terms of the property owner's utility connection-loan contract), Nairobi informal settlements.
comparator_definition: Disconnection-eligible control compounds exempted from enforcement (ad hoc/no systematic disconnection).
effect_measure: Randomized controlled trial, intent-to-treat regression estimates with robust standard errors, 9-month follow-up survey plus 5 years of daily administrative billing panel data
effect_estimate: Payment likelihood within one month increased by 30 percentage points from an 11-percentage-point control base (p<0.001); total payments increased by US$8.80 from a US$5.02 base (p<0.001). Water-access outcomes at 9-month endline: piped water/sanitation connection rates statistically indistinguishable between treatment and control (most of 96 disconnected compounds reconnected after partial payment); main water source = piped water 4.4 percentage points higher in treatment, not significant (p=0.243); monthly water spending Control US$6.62 vs Treatment US$6.86 (p=0.803); weekly water-collection time Control 118 min vs Treatment 100 min (p=0.388) -- a precisely estimated null effect of contract enforcement on actual household water access.
sample_size: field experiment across Nairobi informal-settlement compounds with utility connection loans; 96 disconnected compounds in enforcement arm; 5-year daily billing panel (2014-2018) plus 9-month post-intervention survey
direction: positive and significant for payment compliance; null (no significant effect) for water access, connection rates, spending and collection time
adjusted: adjusted (randomized design with baseline balance checks; robust standard errors)

exposure_definition: Household formal connection status to the municipal water utility (Baguio Water District, BWD): own household metered connection, requiring an upfront PHP 10,000-14,000 (US$234-327) connection fee plus installation cost.

Shared/other BWD connection vs. none: -20.8% decrease in consumption but 2.71x odds of affordability.
direction: positive and significant across all four water-security outcomes for own household connection
adjusted: adjusted (household size as control variable; financial, physical, and social resource covariates)

exposure_definition: Rural municipality implements a small-scale water supply system through a community-based water user association (WUA) -- a participatory institutional/legal management model -- versus
comparator_definition: Rural municipality implements a small-scale water supply system through non-participatory local government management (the referent/control project type).
effect_measure: Difference-in-differences estimator combined with kernel propensity-score matching, Brazilian census panel (2000, 2010) plus national water and sanitation survey
effect_estimate: Municipalities with WUA-managed projects realized piped-water access-rate increases of approximately 6 percentage points above the national average trend (statistically significant, robust to specification changes and matching-balance checks). Rural piped-water access rose from a 15-16% baseline (2000) to 33.4% in WUA-served areas versus 24.9% in local-government-served areas by 2010. Heterogeneity analysis: in local-government-project municipalities with independently higher accountability (local media presence, political competition, or pre-implementation citizen mobilization), access-rate gains matched WUA-area gains, indicating participatory accountability -- not project type per se -- is the underlying mechanism.
sample_size: national municipality-level panel, Brazil (2000-2010 census plus national water/sanitation survey)
direction: positive and significant (WUA/participatory management increases piped-water access rates)
adjusted: adjusted (kernel propensity-score matching on determinants of project-type choice, informed by semi-structured expert interviews; robustness checks confirm no structural treatment/control differences)

Difference-in-differences with kernel matching directly isolating a specific institutional/legal management-model mechanism (community-based water user association vs. non-participatory local government management) with piped-water access rate as the directly measured water-access outcome -- a genuine Family A (legal recognition/formal connection) estimate at national administrative-panel scale.

exposure_definition: Residential customers of a municipally-owned water utility subject to state public utility commission (PUC) economic regulation (in the five U.S. states that regulated municipal water rate structures at the state level), United States, 1965 AWWA survey data.
comparator_definition: Residential customers of a municipally-owned water utility subject to local-only economic regulation (regulated by city council or water commission, not by a state public utility commission).
effect_measure: Monopoly welfare loss as percent of residential customer's annual water bill (two-sample mean difference, t-test)
effect_estimate: Model 1 (unweighted average): locally-regulated 9.6% (SE 0.583, n=88) vs. state-regulated 5.2% (SE 0.818, n=27); difference -4.6 percentage points, t=-4.58 (p<0.01, one-tailed). direction: negative (state-level economic regulation associated with lower excess pricing / lower monopoly welfare loss, i.e., improved affordability, relative to local-only regulation)
